briefing.text: Total cholesterol may be recorded in mixed units across hospital sites (mmol/L vs mg/dL) even though the column description says mg/dL; at least one row shows a value like 5.77, which is a mmol/L value, and haemoglobin values around 156 look like g/L rather than g/dL. Before comparing groups, tabulate TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL (and HEMOGLOBIN, SERUM_ALBUMIN) by SITE and look for bimodality (values ~3-9 vs ~120-350). If found, convert to a single unit per site (mmol/L x 38.67 = mg/dL) and report the comparison both before and after harmonisation.
briefing.reason: A unit mix that differs by site can create or reverse a group difference in cholesterol on its own; comparing unharmonised values could give the wrong label.

briefing.text: Site both enrolled patients and ran the blood tests, so site can confound the ER-status vs cholesterol comparison (different ER-negative mix and different lab calibration or units by site, i.e. Simpson's paradox risk). Cross-tabulate ER_STATUS by SITE and cholesterol by SITE; compare within site (stratified test or regression cholesterol ~ ER_STATUS + SITE) and check the direction is consistent across sites.
briefing.reason: If ER mix differs by site and cholesterol levels differ by site, the pooled comparison can point in a different direction from the within-site comparison.

briefing.text: Cholesterol may contain implausible values, sentinel codes (e.g. 0, 999, -1) or missing entries, and it is right-skewed. Describe its range and missingness by ER group (after unit harmonisation), drop physiologically impossible values, and use both Welch t-test and Mann-Whitney, reporting the effect size with a confidence interval rather than only a p-value.
briefing.reason: A few sentinel or outlier values can drive a mean difference; robust tests and effect sizes protect the conclusion.

briefing.text: The sample table may hold several samples per patient (e.g. primary plus metastasis), so joining it to the patient table duplicates patients and inflates n. Count rows per PATIENT_ID in each file; cholesterol and ER status are patient-level variables, so analyse one row per patient.
briefing.reason: Pseudoreplication from a naive join would overstate significance and over-weight some patients.

briefing.text: ER_STATUS may disagree with ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE (e.g. status positive with 0%, or negative with >=1%), or contain missing/odd codes. Cross-tabulate ER_STATUS against ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE >= 1% (ASCO/CAP threshold), exclude unclear codes, and run a sensitivity analysis with ER defined from the percentage.
briefing.reason: Misclassified exposure groups can dilute or distort the comparison; checking robustness to the ER definition matters for the label.

briefing.text: Age, sex and BMI are associated with cholesterol and with ER status (ER-negative tumours are more common in younger patients; cholesterol rises with age). Compare these by ER group and, as a sensitivity analysis, fit cholesterol ~ ER + site + age + sex + BMI to see whether the direction holds.
briefing.reason: Adjustment for known confounders checks that any observed difference is not explained by demographic imbalance.

briefing.text: The hypothesis is directional (ER-negative higher). Report the sign of the ER-negative minus ER-positive difference with its CI after unit and site handling. A clear difference in the opposite direction contradicts the claim; and because the relevant variables exist, the 'Not verifiable' label applies only if they are truly absent or unusable, not merely because a result is non-significant.
briefing.reason: Prevents mislabelling: direction and the meaning of each label must be applied correctly once the analysis is done.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat the C1 unit problem as the only data-quality issue; neither shows a per-row check that no individual C2/C3 cholesterol value is in mmol/L (or that no C1 value is already in mg/dL), only site-level ranges.
Both treat every enrolled patient as in scope regardless of sex (140 of 270 patients are recorded Male) and regardless of whether ER status came from a primary tumour or a metastasis.
Both treat patients as independent and site as a fixed adjustment; with C1 being 80% ER-negative, the pooled estimate leans heavily on the conversion factor and on C1's ER mix.
Both assume age/sex/BMI are the relevant confounders; neither considers performance status (illness severity can lower cholesterol).
unused_evidence: data_clinical_sample.txt: SAMPLE_TYPE (194 Primary, 76 Metastasis), PROCESSING_BATCH and TUMOR_PURITY were not used. If ER status was assessed on the profiled sample, ER calls from metastases may differ from primary ER status; the comparison was not repeated within primary-only patients.
ECOG_PS (supplement) was not used. Patients in poorer condition may have lower cholesterol, and ECOG may differ by ER group.
FOLLOW_UP_MONTHS was not used; it is probably irrelevant to a cross-sectional baseline cholesterol comparison.
HEMOGLOBIN/SERUM_ALBUMIN were used only to support the unit diagnosis. Neither team checked whether their own unit issues hide row-level inconsistencies.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams' weakest point (that all C1 values are mmol/L) was argued from the site range and from within-site comparisons. That is reasonable, but neither team reported a row-level check for values outside the expected range in each site.
Team A recorded 'age/sex/BMI confounding: found_in_data false' but did not report the balance tables. Team B adjusted for age and sex but not BMI.
second_readings: 'Patients with ER-negative tumours': ER status could be defined from ER_STATUS or from ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE at a 1% or 10% cut-off. The two agree perfectly here (0% vs >0%), so this does not matter.

'Higher total cholesterol' could mean the mean, the median, or the cohort as observed (pooled) versus within site. Both teams report all of these and they agree, so the second reading does not change the claim.
The scope could be restricted to female patients or to primary-tumour samples; neither team tested these restrictions.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed answer fairly well. The ER coding (0 = negative, matching ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE) and the C1 unit fix both check out against the data, and within-site comparisons do not depend on the conversion. The remaining risks are the sample-type and ECOG evidence that neither team used, and the cohort's scope (sex, primary vs metastasis), none of which seems likely to flip a difference that is consistent across all sites.

Does the direction or its precision differ from the full cohort, and does that change which population your method should report on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate ECOG_PS by ER group and add it to your adjusted model. Show the age/sex/BMI balance by ER group that supports 'found_in_data: false'. Does either change the estimate or your choice of covariates?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Repeat the comparison separately in Female and Male patients, and flag any individual cholesterol value that falls outside the range typical for its site's unit (C1 rows above about 15, C2/C3 rows below about 20). Do either of these checks change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your adjusted model omits BMI and ECOG_PS from the supplement table. Add them and tabulate them by ER group. Does the adjusted ER coefficient move enough to change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Repeat the within-site comparison within each sex, and run a row-level unit check (any C2/C3 value below about 20 or any C1 value above about 15). Does either check reveal mixed units or a sex-specific pattern that would change your method?

findings.question: How often does oestrogen receptor status differ between a primary breast tumour and its metastasis? In which direction does it usually change (positive to negative or the reverse)?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 502/403 on all 4 calls (3 searches, 1 contents), so no page was read. From background knowledge only: ER discordance between primary and metastasis occurs in roughly 10-20% of patients (pooled estimates ~14-20%), mostly positive-to-negative (ER loss) rather than negative-to-positive. Metastatic-sample ER calls would therefore tend to inflate the ER-negative group; restricting to primary samples is a reasonable sensitivity analysis.

findings.question: Is serum total cholesterol known to fall with worse performance status or advanced cancer, so that it would confound a comparison between tumour subtypes?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: gateway unavailable, no page was read. From background knowledge only: yes, low total cholesterol is commonly reported in advanced or metastatic cancer, cachexia and poor nutritional or functional status, and it goes along with low albumin and worse performance status. ECOG confounds the comparison only if it also differs between ER groups, so check ECOG by ER group. If it differs, add ECOG (and stage or metastatic status) in an adjusted sensitivity model.
